match.reason: The closest bank point, Floods and tropical cyclones, is a broader card that splits its focus between floods and cyclones, and its questions test flood causes, so it does not teach the cyclone-only idea in this brief, which also covers the warm-ocean formation and the November to April northern Australian season.

draft.title: Tropical cyclones
card: A tropical cyclone is a huge spinning storm. It forms over warm ocean water near the equator, in the tropics.
Warm sea water feeds the storm with heat and moisture. When a cyclone moves over cooler water or onto land, it loses that supply and weakens.
Cyclones bring three main dangers: destructive winds, heavy rain, and storm surges. A storm surge is a rise in sea level that pushes water onto the coast.
In Australia, cyclones mostly hit northern areas, such as Queensland, the Northern Territory and northern Western Australia. The cyclone season runs from November to April.
draft.remember: Cyclones form over warm tropical seas and bring wind, rain and storm surges to northern Australia from November to April.

a.q: Why does a tropical cyclone usually weaken after it moves over land?
opts: It loses the warm ocean water that feeds it
It gains too much heat from the dry ground
It is pushed back out to sea by storm surges
It runs out of rain because land is too flat
a.why: A cyclone gets its heat and moisture from warm ocean water. Over land that supply is cut off, so the storm weakens. Storm surges are a danger the cyclone causes, not something that pushes it back.
a.clue: Think about what feeds the storm.

b.q: Layla lives in Townsville, Queensland. In which months should her family be most ready for a tropical cyclone?
b.why: Cyclone season in northern Australia runs from November to April, so that is when Layla's family should be ready. Winter months are outside the season. A cyclone can arrive in any month of the season, not only January.
b.clue: Cyclone season spans the warm, wet half of the year.

a.best: It loses the warm ocean water that feeds it
